transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

I've been hearing voices that other people tell me aren't there, and it's really starting to scare me. This has been going on for about seven months now. I just don't understand why this is happening to me.
Have you had periods where you felt unusually high, irritable, or depressed for several days or more, along with the voices?
No, I haven't really experienced times where I felt unusually high, irritable, or depressed like that. It's mostly just been the voices, and I'm not sure I've had those kinds of mood shifts at all.
Besides the voices, have you ever had strong beliefs that others say aren't true—like being convinced someone is watching you or that you have a special mission?
No, I don't have any beliefs like that. I don't feel like anyone is watching me or that I have some special mission. It really is just the voices that I keep hearing.
Have the voices been affecting your ability to work, study, or get along with others?

Yes, they've made it almost impossible to focus, and I've lost all motivation to keep up with my studies. I've also been avoiding my family and friends because the voices are so distracting and overwhelming that I just can't handle being around people right now.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["Schizophrenia"], and based on this conversation, this diagnosis remains the most appropriate. The patient reports persistent auditory hallucinations for seven months without mood episodes or manic symptoms, which makes mood disorder with psychotic features less likely. The absence of delusional beliefs rules out Delusional Disorder, and there is no history of trauma or anxiety-focused symptoms to suggest PTSD or anxiety disorders. The presence of psychosis without mood disturbance or functional decline attributable to mood supports Schizophrenia over Schizoaffective Disorder. The significant functional impairment further supports this diagnosis. No new candidate better fits the clinical picture.

Other disorders without psychotic features are ruled out at this stage.

Given the duration (seven months) and the prominence of hallucinations, Schizophrenia remains the most plausible diagnosis at this stage, though further evaluation of disorganized speech, negative symptoms, or functional decline would be needed for confirmation. However, based on current information, it is the only candidate that fits.
